data.title: 3 High-Yield Dividend Stocks to Watch This Thanksgiving
data.description:
Thanksgiving is a good time to review income investments through Dividend Stocks. Three stocks stand out for their high yields: Frontline (FRO), Nordic American Tankers (NAT), and Ares Capital (ARCC). All three pay dividends, but their income profiles differ. Based on TipRanks data, their indicated yields range from about 10% to 13%.

Frontline (FRO)

Frontline operates oil tankers, transporting crude oil and petroleum products. Its earnings depend heavily on shipping rates, which can rise or fall quickly.

The company has a record of quarterly dividends, but payments have varied widely. Its latest declared regular quarterly dividend is $2.38 per share, reflecting a current yield of 12.97%. In 2025, regular quarterly dividends totaled just $0.93, highlighting the risk of relying on peak-cycle payouts.

TipRanks reports a Moderate Buy consensus rating on FRO. The average analyst price target of $58.07 implies 21.9% upside from the November 25 closing price of $47.65.

Nordic American Tankers (NAT)

Nordic American Tankers operates a fleet of Suezmax oil tankers. Its business is exposed to the same freight-rate cycle as Frontline.

NAT paid a dividend of $0.27 per share in its latest reported quarter, implying a current yield of 12.19%. The company has paid quarterly dividends, but the amounts have changed significantly. For example, payments rose from $0.10 in September 2025 to $0.27 in September 2026.

On TipRanks, NAT has a Hold consensus rating with an average analyst price target of $8.50 implying 31.2% upside from the November 25 closing price.

Ares Capital (ARCC)

Ares Capital is a U.S. specialty finance company that lends money to mid-sized businesses. It is not a traditional bank or an asset management company. Its income comes largely from its investment portfolio rather than shipping rates.

ARCC has maintained a $0.48 quarterly dividend throughout 2024, 2025, and 2026. That equals $1.92 annually, with a yield of 10.13%. Its dividend record is more stable than those of the tanker companies, although credit losses could still affect future payments.

On TipRanks, ARCC has a Strong Buy consensus rating with the average analyst price target of $20.42 implying 7.7% upside from the November 25 closing price.

data.title: Salesforce Stock (CRM) Looks Mispriced After the AI Sell-Off
data.description:
Salesforce (CRM) stock looks mispriced after the recent software sell-off, driven by fears that artificial intelligence (AI) will disrupt traditional enterprise software. The customer relationship management software provider enters this stretch from a position of financial strength, having generated $14.4 billion in free cash flow in Fiscal 2026. In the company’s second-quarter Fiscal 2027 earnings release in August 2026, Chair and CEO Marc Benioff addressed the AI opportunity and pushed back against the disruption narrative, stating, “AI is delivering value across every layer of our platform.”

I think investors are overlooking how little physical investment Salesforce needs to pursue that opportunity, with capex projected at roughly 1.5% of revenue in Fiscal 2027. Rather than being replaced, its software can become more useful and more embedded as enterprises adopt autonomous AI agents across workflows, in my view. Yet the market seems far more concerned about disruption. Ahead of the company’s third-quarter earnings report on December 2, I rate CRM a Buy.

AI Exposure Without the Infrastructure Bill

What I like about Salesforce is that it offers AI exposure without the huge infrastructure bill. Now, Monday’s rally following Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia (NVDA) lifted CRM 2.7%. Yet shares remain roughly 26% below their August post-earnings level. Investors have sold software alongside companies facing enormous graphics processing unit (GPU) and power commitments, but Salesforce’s spending requirements look very different.

For context, Salesforce’s Fiscal 2026 operating cash flow reached $15 billion, with FCF of $14.4 billion. However, physical capex consumed only about 4% of operating cash. Its most recent Q2 FY27 results repeated the pattern, with $1.3 billion of operating cash and $1.1 billion of FCF.

We are seeing that Salesforce can keep developing Agentforce without committing tens of billions to new data centers. That leaves more flexibility for shareholder-friendly capital allocation, including ongoing share buybacks and its quarterly dividend. I find that appealing, especially as infrastructure financing has become such a concern elsewhere in the technology sector.

In addition, I have grown fond of AIforce, which also gives Salesforce a sensible response to changing interfaces. Customers can access its data and take governed actions through outside assistants. Following August’s Claudeforce integration with Anthropic’s (ANT) Claude, Salesforce teamed up with Microsoft (MSFT) last week to launch Copilotforce, bringing Salesforce workflows into Microsoft Copilot (now in public beta) and Teams (currently in pilot).

So an employee can change where they work while continuing to use Salesforce underneath. I actually find that more reassuring than simply insisting customers will keep opening traditional CRM screens.

CRM’s Q3 Could Show More AI Payoff

I believe CRM’s Q3 could show more AI payoff when Salesforce reports on December 2. Management guided to $11.42–$11.50 billion of revenue, representing 11%–12% growth. Consensus sits around $11.46 billion, with adjusted earnings per share (EPS) forecast of $3.45. The roughly 14% constant-currency growth outlook for current remaining performance obligations (cRPO) gives me another reason to expect solid subscription demand. I will watch whether bookings support management’s promised organic reacceleration.

Last quarter, Agentforce annual recurring revenue (ARR), now including Slackbot and Headless 360, exceeded $1.5 billion, growing over 240% year-over-year. Agentforce and Data 360 combined ARR approached $3.9 billion. Agentic Work Units increased 97% sequentially, while premium Agentforce bookings more than doubled sequentially. Data 360 ingested 104 trillion records, up 355% year-over-year.

These figures suggest customers are putting agents into production and using the supporting data infrastructure. I want to see that usage keep converting into larger contracts.

I also find it interesting that Slack’s net-new annual order value delivered its fastest quarterly growth since acquisition. Slackbot gives Salesforce another familiar place to sell AI capabilities. Copilotforce widens distribution further. Each additional agent can bring consumption revenue from an existing customer. Data 360 can grow alongside it as those agents access more company information.

Beyond Q3, the pending Braze (BRZE) acquisition could expand marketing opportunities once it closes. Security offers another avenue through Salesforce Guardian. With $66.3 billion of remaining performance obligations, Salesforce has time to develop these businesses. I think steady expansion within existing accounts can support healthy growth well into 2027.

CRM’s Valuation Looks Too Pessimistic

Following the stock’s recent sell-off, CRM’s valuation looks too pessimistic. Still, the bear case deserves attention. It’s true that organic growth is much slower than in Salesforce’s earlier years. Informatica contributes slightly over four percentage points to Q3’s revenue growth outlook. Organic growth could remain stuck in the high single digits.

AI could weaken per-seat pricing, and competition from Microsoft or ServiceNow (NOW) remains intense. Buying more businesses also complicates growth comparisons. Integrating Informatica and Braze will demand attention, while Agentforce adoption could disappoint.

However, at today’s price levels, I think investors are already allowing for a lot to go wrong. CRM trades at 11.1x January 2027 adjusted earnings and 11.6x January 2028 adjusted earnings. The multiples fall to 10.0x for January 2029 and 8.7x for January 2030. FY2028 consensus is subdued, following an investment-gain boost to FY2027 earnings.

Q2 alone included $2.53 per share from those gains. I therefore put more weight on FY2028’s cleaner base. Rather than a return to 20% revenue growth, I believe low-double-digit growth with controlled costs can still deliver good per-share returns. So paying 11.6x that estimate looks unusually attractive for recurring software revenue with strong margins.

Capital returns add to the appeal. Salesforce’s $25 billion accelerated share repurchase (ASR) initially delivered 103 million shares, substantially reducing the share base. Debt financed that transaction, so repeating it annually would be unrealistic. Still, ongoing cash generation can support further repurchases. At these multiples, each buyback dollar retires considerably more earnings than at past premium valuations.

The quarterly $0.44 dividend adds a smaller cash return. Steady growth alongside a declining share count can lift EPS even if we don’t see a major rerating. Better confidence in Agentforce would provide additional upside.

Wall Street Sees Substantial Upside

Wall Street sees substantial upside, with a Strong Buy consensus from 30 Buy and nine Hold ratings. On TipRanks, the average CRM price target of $276.64 implies roughly 43% upside from today’s share price.

Conclusion

Salesforce needs to prove that AI can improve organic growth. I think its recent adoption figures and outside integrations give it a credible chance. Meanwhile, modest capex preserves a large pool of cash for shareholders. At roughly 11.6x next fiscal year’s earnings, investors have room for slower progress. I remain Bullish ahead of Q3.

data.title: Pfizer (PFE) Has the Highest Yield, but Which Pharma Stock Offers a Better Dividend?
data.description:
Pfizer (PFE) offers one of the highest dividend yields among large-cap healthcare stocks, but a higher yield does not always mean a better dividend. Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) and AbbVie (ABBV) also pay dividends, with different levels of dividend growth, business stability, and payout risk. We compare the three stocks using the TipRanks Stock Comparison tool to see which offers the better dividend opportunity.

Beyond dividends, the tool also allows us to compare stocks based on analyst consensus, price target, market cap, TipRanks Smart Score, and more. Let us look at how Pfizer, Johnson & Johnson, and AbbVie compare on some of these metrics. Notably, all three stocks offer dividend yields above the healthcare sector average of 1.423%. Also, all three have a TipRanks Smart Score of 7.

1. Pfizer (PFE) — Pfizer Inc. is a global biopharmaceutical company that develops and manufactures prescription medicines and vaccines across oncology, immunology, cardiology, and infectious diseases, led by blockbuster franchises like blood thinner Eliquis, the Prevnar vaccine line, and cancer therapies such as Padcev. It is navigating a post-COVID transition, with its stock trading well below 2021 highs. In the Q2 2026 earnings call, the company raised its full-year 2026 revenue outlook to $62–$64 billion.

The biopharma company offers a 6.04% dividend yield and a 245.71% payout ratio, which looks high because of restructuring costs and acquisition-related write-offs. It pays a quarterly dividend of $0.43 per share and has maintained the rate through 2025 and 2026. Looking ahead, U.S. patents on Eliquis, Ibrance, and Xtandi expire in 2027, with generic Eliquis entry set for April 2028. Together, the three drugs generated about 23% of Pfizer’s 2025 revenue. While these losses could weigh on cash flow and limit near-term dividend increases, recent November agreements with Starna and Blackstone (BX), as per Pfizer’s website, show it is actively investing in its next wave of pipeline therapies.

Wall Street analysts covering PFE stock give it a consensus Hold consensus rating, with 14 analysts rating it a Hold, six rating it a Buy, and one rating it a Hold. On TipRanks, the average PFE stock price target of $30.28 implies a 6.39% upside.

2. Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) — Johnson & Johnson operates across innovative pharmaceuticals and medical devices. Strong demand for its newer cancer and immunology drugs has pushed full-year 2026 sales guidance to a midpoint of $101.2 billion. According to the Johnson & Johnson website, the company is also expanding its pipeline, marked by November’s Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval of head-and-neck cancer therapy Rybrevant Faspro and a $2.2 billion deal to acquire Ollin Biosciences.

The healthcare giant is a dividend aristocrat, having increased its annual shareholder dividend every year for more than six consecutive decades. It offers a 1.92% dividend yield and a payout ratio of 80.73%. The company reported annual free cash flow of roughly $20 billion in 2025 and has returned more than 65% of its five-year free cash flow to shareholders through dividends and buybacks. In its Q3 2026 earnings call, Johnson & Johnson guided to roughly $21 billion in full-year free cash flow, suggesting it can maintain steady annual dividend increases.

On TipRanks, JNJ has a Moderate Buy consensus with 11 Buy and six Hold ratings. The average stock price target of $289.88 represents 4.85% upside from the last price.

3. AbbVie (ABBV) — AbbVie is a biopharmaceutical company focused on immunology, neuroscience, oncology, and aesthetics, led by major brands like Skyrizi, Rinvoq, and Botox. Rapid sales growth in its newer immunology and neuroscience drugs lifted full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $67.8 billion, as reported during its third-quarter earnings call. The FDA approval of Rinvoq for vitiligo earlier this week is another growth catalyst.

The company offers a 2.30% dividend yield and a 120.65% payout ratio. While accounting charges push that ratio above 100%, AbbVie generated $14 billion in free cash flow during the first nine months of 2026, covering its dividend obligations. In October 2026, the board approved a 5.2% quarterly dividend increase, lifting the payout from $1.73 to $1.82 per share starting in February 2027.

Among the three names, AbbVie is the only one carrying a Strong Buy consensus rating from Wall Street analysts on TipRanks. 18 analysts rate it a Buy, while four rate it a Hold. The average ABBV price target of $314.62 suggests a 4.78% upside.

Conclusion

Pfizer offers the highest yield among the three stocks, but a better dividend depends on more than yield alone. Johnson & Johnson offers greater stability and a long record of dividend increases, while AbbVie combines a meaningful yield with a history of dividend growth. data.title: Alibaba Stock (BABA) Looks Cheap Until You Follow the Cash
data.description:
Alibaba (BABA) stock looks cheap until you follow the cash. The Chinese e-commerce and cloud provider burned $5.1 billion in Q2 2027. CFO Toby Xu said management is “targeting to achieve positive free cash flow.” I welcome that focus, but investors once bought BABA for its enormous excess cash.

Today, shareholders face the risks of an expensive artificial intelligence (AI) buildout under tightening U.S. restrictions. With American technology stocks also falling, I see less reason to accept Alibaba’s additional risks. Therefore, I rate BABA stock a Sell despite its seemingly attractive earnings multiple.

Cash Generation Is Falling Short

Alibaba’s cash generation is falling short even as its cloud business improves. To be fair, last week’s Q2 results offered plenty for bulls. Total revenue grew 10%. AI Cloud and Compute Services revenue climbed 53%, with external revenue up 64%. Cloud adjusted EBITA increased 121%, lifting its margin to 14.5%.

Also, AI-related product revenue has now grown at triple-digit rates for 13 consecutive quarters. These figures show genuine demand and improving profitability.

However, operating cash flow of RMB15.7 billion ($2.34 billion) was offset by capex of RMB50.5 billion ($7.53 billion). Free cash flow (FCF) was negative RMB34.5 billion ($5.14 billion). That followed outflows of RMB44.7 billion ($6.58 billion) in June and RMB17.3 billion ($2.51 billion) in March. September improved sequentially, and operating cash flow rose 55% year-over-year. Yet spending still overwhelmed the cash coming in.

First-half FCF outflows reached RMB79.1 billion (about $11.8 billion), nearly doubling year-over-year. Capex totaled RMB118.1 billion ($17.62 billion) across those six months.

These investments could build a highly valuable cloud business. I understand why Alibaba wants more capacity while customers are asking for it. Yet shareholders need returns after paying for that equipment. Rising accounting profits offer limited reassurance when cash available for distributions keeps disappearing into infrastructure.

Procurement timing can move spending between quarters. Three consecutive FCF outflows make this harder to dismiss as a quarterly timing issue. Management expects overall cash flow to turn positive in the second half of calendar year 2028. That doesn’t indicate how much, or whether it will be sustainable.

Chip Restrictions Complicate the AI Expansion

Chip restrictions complicate the AI expansion just as Alibaba is spending hardest. The most recently updated U.S. rules impose licensing requirements on certain overseas data centers supplying advanced compute to Chinese companies. They also tighten foundry checks. Renting capacity abroad is becoming harder, even when the hardware never enters China. This creates another obstacle to turning Alibaba’s cloud demand into revenue.

CEO Eddie Wu said the restrictions would affect next year’s products and services. He suggested cloud growth could run at 30%-45% in Fiscal 2028 beginning in 2027, while stressing that the assessment remains ongoing. That would still be impressive growth. However, it would also represent a slowdown from the latest quarter. Management expects domestic computing capacity to support renewed acceleration in 2028, but investors must fund the transition before knowing its outcome.

Lastly, one could argue that T-Head and Qwen give Alibaba credible domestic technology. Its Zhenwu V900 chip is scheduled for commercial release in Q1 2027. However, chip design cannot instantly create more foundry capacity. Existing controls on manufacturing equipment and high-bandwidth memory also complicate domestic alternatives. U.S. hyperscalers face supply constraints, but fewer barriers to buying leading hardware.

China’s shifting policy environment adds uncertainty. Additionally, ADR buyers own a Cayman holding company, and some regulated operations rely on contractual variable interest entity (VIE) control. That adds legal risk beyond the usual uncertainties of an AI investment cycle.

A Low P/E Is an Incomplete Answer

Alibaba’s low P/E is an incomplete answer to these cash-flow concerns. Today, BABA trades at 13.15x Fiscal 2027 earnings per share (EPS) of $6.54. The multiple falls to 9.41x Fiscal 2028 EPS of $9.14 and 7.41x Fiscal 2029 EPS of $11.61. That is a substantial discount to American technology leaders. Yet those estimates already assume a strong earnings recovery and say little about how much cash shareholders can receive after AI spending.

Recent capital returns reinforce my caution. Quarterly buybacks totaled just $221 million, while the dividend yields roughly 1.3%. Meanwhile, Alibaba issued 710 million ordinary shares to raise HK$80 billion. The weighted-average basic share count increased year-over-year. This strengthens funding, but existing investors now share future profits with a larger shareholder base.

Alibaba’s roughly $73 billion of cash and liquid investments provides substantial protection. Still, it also gives management considerable room to keep spending before cash returns improve.

I find the opportunity cost increasingly difficult to ignore after the technology sell-off. Amazon (AMZN), the closest e-commerce-and-cloud comparison, trades at 23.93x 2027 earnings. Alphabet (GOOGL) trades at 18.94x next year’s EPS. Microsoft (MSFT) trades at 24.59x Fiscal 2027 earnings, falling to 20x Fiscal 2028 earnings. These multiples are notably higher than Alibaba’s, but I think the premium is worth paying.

Investors get exceptional businesses with fewer restrictions on advanced AI hardware. They also avoid the additional policy and ownership risks attached to Chinese equities. Following the sell-off, their valuations look reasonable enough that I see little reason to accept those extra uncertainties. Alibaba could outperform if its investments pay off and restrictions ease.

Yet a lower P/E alone doesn’t make it the more attractive investment. I’d rather pay more for the quality and greater predictability available from its U.S. peers.

Wall Street Remains Bullish

Wall Street remains bullish despite these concerns. TipRanks shows a Strong Buy consensus from 16 unanimous Buy ratings. The average price target of $172.13 implies 100% upside from today’s price levels. My cash flow concerns leave me considerably less optimistic.

Conclusion

Alibaba could prove very cheap if cloud growth produces sustained free cash flow. Its financial resources may give it time, and domestic chips could reduce foreign dependence. Yet I still want evidence that shareholders will benefit from this spending. With cash returns subdued and hardware restrictions tightening, the low P/E leaves me unconvinced. I prefer the stronger shareholder economics available elsewhere.

data.title: Nike (NKE) Targets a Turnaround with Ambitious Fiscal 2031 Goals
data.description:
Nike (NKE) is targeting a major turnaround with ambitious Fiscal 2031 goals, and the stock’s current valuation reflects only a fraction of the long-term earnings potential those goals imply. Shares of the sportswear maker have fallen more than 40% in 2026, impacted by a mix of company-specific issues such as negative revenue growth and weak earnings momentum, as well as macro headwinds like high energy prices that weigh on discretionary consumer spending.

In response, the company has laid out a plan to generate $5 billion in incremental revenue and an adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $3–$3.50 by Fiscal 2031 (the company’s financial year ends in May).

On near-term numbers, the stock doesn’t look cheap. The elevated 26.8x multiple on management’s expected Fiscal 2027 EPS of about $1.35 suggests the market is already pricing in some earnings recovery. However, the picture changes against the longer-term target, implying that the market is giving credit for only part of the expansion projected for the years after Fiscal 2027.

I rate Nike a speculative Buy. While hitting ambitious financial targets is far from certain, the shares appear somewhat undervalued should Nike achieve the $3.25 midpoint of its Fiscal 2031 EPS outlook. Coupled with the company’s aspiration to return $12 billion to shareholders as the turnaround unfolds, I think the shares offer enough value at current prices.

Nike’s New Fiscal 2031 Targets

Nike used its Investor Day, held on November 17, 2026, to announce its new “Full Stride Ahead” strategy. Its key elements include ambitious Fiscal 2031 targets, most notably $5 billion in incremental revenue and an adjusted EPS of $3–$3.50.

Let us use the $42.8 billion analyst estimate for Fiscal 2027 as a starting point to evaluate management’s top-line ambitions. Assuming Nike hits its $5 billion incremental revenue target, we see that annual revenue growth should amount to just under 3% per year, indicating limited volume growth and sales rising largely in line with inflation. While this may seem rather unambitious, it would represent the company’s fastest top-line expansion since Fiscal 2023, when sales increased 9.65%.

For earnings, the projected improvement is much more pronounced. Using Nike’s forecast of adjusted EPS of about $1.35 in Fiscal 2027, the $3–$3.50 adjusted Fiscal 2031 EPS target implies about 25% annual earnings growth at the $3.25 EPS midpoint. I think this is quite ambitious given the modest revenue aspirations outlined above.

Before we dive into the details behind these numbers in the next section, I believe the key takeaway for readers is that the “Full Stride Ahead” strategy is centered around earnings growth, with revenue expansion playing a secondary role in my opinion. That said, I think the sales targets in particular are quite achievable, supporting my Buy rating on the shares.

Nike’s Revenue and Earnings Drivers

Now that we have seen the key numbers behind Nike’s new strategy, let’s discuss how the company plans to get there. Given the modest projected revenue expansion of marginally below 3% per year over the “Full Stride Ahead” horizon, I think achieving margin improvements will ultimately determine Nike’s turnaround success.

For Fiscal 2027, the company anticipates delivering an adjusted operating margin of about 6%. By the end of Fiscal 2031, the number should be closer to 12%–14%, implying a dramatic improvement. Avenues for margin improvement include simplifying and standardizing processes to improve execution and productivity, implementing integrated planning across demand, inventory, supply, and financial decisions, and building a more flexible, responsive supply network.

Nike also targets greater use of technology and artificial intelligence (AI) to improve decision-making, speed, and efficiency. As such, the road to higher margins for Nike entails both improving the efficiency of existing processes and making the most of new technologies such as AI to drive incremental improvements.

While margin expansion is expected to do the heavy lifting for EPS growth, Nike also expects a turnaround in sales momentum. Here, the company is focusing on 23 priority countries, which will drive over 90% of the anticipated $5 billion revenue growth. Nike anticipates higher sales by scaling breakthrough innovations into platforms that reach more athletes across more sports, as well as working with marketplace partners to tailor product assortments and experiences to local athletes.

To sum up, Nike’s earnings growth is likely to come primarily from efficiency gains and associated margin expansion, with higher revenues playing a complementary role. While the absolute level of margin improvement may seem too ambitious at first, achieving 12%–14% operating margins is certainly doable for an efficiently run company, supporting my Buy rating on Nike.

Nike’s Valuation

Nike shares trade at 26.8x expected Fiscal 2027 adjusted EPS of $1.35, implying the market is giving the company some credit for anticipated medium-term earnings growth. For comparison, the equal-weight Invesco S&P 500 index (RSP) trades at a much lower valuation of about 16.6x forward earnings.

I think the equal-weight Invesco S&P 500 is a good benchmark for Nike, as the company’s market cap has slumped to only $53 billion after declines in the 2026 share price. This is well below the large-cap stocks that dominate the market-cap-weighted S&P 500 index (SPX), which trades at a higher valuation.

My view on Nike is that it will outperform equal-weight Invesco S&P 500 peers only if it hits at least the midpoint of its $3-$3.50 adjusted EPS target for 2031. This potential outperformance comes as Nike may deliver about 25% annual EPS growth over the next four years, notably above the approximate 8.5% EPS growth I expect for the equal-weight Invesco S&P 500.

At the $3.25 midpoint of the Fiscal 2031 EPS outlook, the current share price works out to roughly 11x earnings, suggesting the bigger earnings gains planned for later years are only partly reflected in today’s valuation. This supports a speculative Buy rating on Nike, as the market appears to be giving the company very little credit for its medium-term earnings recovery.

Another positive factor in the Nike investment case is management’s commitment to its dividend, forecasting $12 billion in cumulative dividend returns between Fiscal 2027 and Fiscal 2031. Investors should note, however, that the $0.41 per share quarterly dividend is not covered by projected Fiscal 2027 adjusted EPS of $1.35. The silver lining is that dividend coverage should steadily improve as Nike executes its turnaround plan.

Wall Street’s Take on Nike

On Wall Street, Nike has a Hold consensus rating, based on nine Buy, 18 Hold, and 10 Sell ratings over the past three months. The 12-month average Nike price target is currently $36.73, implying 1.17% upside.

Conclusion

After disastrous 2026 share price performance, Nike is implementing the “Full Stride Ahead” strategy to improve sales and profitability. While the strategy does envisage some revenue expansion, the bulk of the anticipated earnings growth is projected to come from higher margins.

The market remains somewhat skeptical of Nike’s turnaround, with the shares trading at 26.8x expected Fiscal 2027 earnings. While this may seem high relative to immediate peers in the equal-weight Invesco S&P 500 index, it gives the company little credit for its projected nearly 25% EPS growth over the next four years.

I rate Nike a speculative Buy, as the shares should outperform peers if the company hits its new financial targets. That said, the new strategy carries execution risks, so outsized returns are far from guaranteed.

While Fiscal 2031 is still far off, Nike aims to return $12 billion to shareholders in the meantime, potentially making it an interesting play for income investors as the company works on its turnaround. As such, I think Nike stock may appeal to income investors as well as growth investors.

data.title: Coca-Cola Stock (KO) May Struggle to Repeat Its Strong 2026 Performance
data.description:
Coca-Cola (KO) stock may struggle to repeat its strong 2026 performance, as reported revenue growth could slow next year and its valuation leaves limited room for further gains. Shares of the beverage maker have soared in 2026, with investors cheering accelerating revenue and earnings growth after a weak 2025. Indeed, Coca-Cola’s 7% Q3 2026 revenue expansion was notably higher than the 2% net revenue growth for full-year 2025. However, the planned sale of its Africa bottling business is expected to weigh on reported sales in 2027.

Analysts still expect earnings per share (EPS) to grow nearly 6% to $3.53 next year, but Coca-Cola’s shares already trade at 28.19x expected 2027 earnings. While the stock offers investors exposure beyond the artificial intelligence (AI) growth theme, I believe this premium valuation limits its upside. I maintain a Hold rating on KO.

Coca-Cola Regains Revenue Momentum

To understand why Coca-Cola stock has appreciated so much in 2026, we must put the recent rally into context. Coca-Cola ended 2025 with 2% revenue growth, the weakest since 2020, when the COVID-19 pandemic heavily impacted beverage sales.

As such, Coca-Cola’s valuation going into 2026 largely reflected a slow-growing company aiming for incremental margin expansion to drive EPS growth.

Against this backdrop, investors cheered the company’s 7% Q3 2026 revenue increase, as it signals Coca-Cola may command a higher valuation as top-line momentum accelerates. Strong Q3 2026 sales gains were driven by an outsized 25% revenue increase in Latin America, while the main North American market grew sales by only 3% year-over-year.

Indeed, the company notes that emerging and developing markets will remain a key revenue driver for Coca-Cola, as the company only has a 6% share in those markets, less than half the 14% share Coca-Cola boasts in developed markets.

The takeaway for investors is that after a few years of decelerating sales momentum, Coca-Cola has managed to turn around its performance, boosted by strong growth in emerging markets. The relative disappointment comes when we look at analyst estimates for 2027 revenues, where the $48.9 billion consensus number implies a 3.07% decline relative to the strong performance in 2026.

This near-term headwind, partly driven by the sale of the bottling business in Africa, arguably supports my Hold rating on Coca-Cola, despite expected solid sales momentum over the medium to long term.

Coca-Cola’s Earnings Continue to Grow

Coca-Cola reported non-GAAP EPS of $0.91 in Q3 2026, an 11% increase relative to the prior-year quarter. Beyond the higher revenues mentioned above, earnings rose because of a small improvement in operating margins, most evident in both underlying and GAAP-reported figures.

More impressively, EPS rose strongly despite no reduction in share count, as Coca-Cola’s buybacks primarily offset employee stock dilution while management prioritized dividends in its shareholder returns. The $0.53 quarterly dividend per share carries a trailing payout ratio of 62.5%.

Strong Q3 2026 performance led to an upward revision in Coca-Cola’s 2026 earnings forecast, now projecting non-GAAP EPS growth of at least 11% for the full year. Analysts estimate 2026 EPS of $3.34, with a nearly 6% increase to $3.53 EPS projected for 2027.

So, even after the outlook for lower 2027 revenues, Coca-Cola’s earnings should continue to expand next year. The company benefits from the sale of its low-margin bottling business in Africa to Coca-Cola HBC (GB:CCH), a separate company that bottles drinks for Coca-Cola.

However, I maintain my Hold rating on KO stock in the near term, even with the positive earnings outlook, as EPS growth is projected to slow from 11% this year to 6% in 2027.

Coca-Cola Valuation

Following strong 2026 gains, Coca-Cola shares now trade at 28.19x analysts’ consensus 2027 EPS of $3.53. Pepsi (PEP) currently trades at 16.98x the 2027 EPS estimate of $8.62. I believe KO’s high multiple is a reflection of two principal drivers. First, a strong rebound from 2025’s sluggishness, with investors pricing in stronger emerging-market volume growth over the coming years.

Second, and perhaps more important in the near term, growth investors have been diversifying away from the AI growth theme in recent months, rewarding steady-growth companies such as Coca-Cola, as well as Apple (AAPL) and Eli Lilly (LLY). The market seems willing to pay a premium valuation for revenue growth above the overall economy, which is not dependent on developments in the AI space.

My Hold rating on Coca-Cola is driven by the following logic. On the one hand, the shares will continue to offer reasonable earnings growth over the medium to long term, which will be especially valuable for growth investors seeking diversification. On the other hand, the strong year-to-date rally has arguably left limited capital-gain upside in the near term, especially given the outlook for a relative slowdown in growth in 2027.

I agree that the 2027 analysts’ consensus numbers largely reflect the one-off effect of the Africa bottling business sale. That said, the non-recurrence of the 2026 FIFA World Cup will also likely weigh on sales next year, especially in Mexico (Coca-Cola’s largest market in Latin America) and North America. Therefore, some near-term caution may be warranted as Coca-Cola will likely face tough comparables when it reports 2027 results.

Wall Street’s Take on Coca-Cola

On Wall Street, Coca-Cola has a Strong Buy consensus rating, based on 13 Buy and three Hold ratings over the past three months. Notably, no analyst sees KO as a Sell. The 12-month average Coca-Cola price target is currently $99.40, implying downside.

Conclusion

Coca-Cola shares have delivered strong returns in 2026, driven by a 7% expansion in Q3 2026 sales, as well as a small double-digit increase in EPS. While EPS is likely to continue growing in 2027, the sale of the Africa bottling business will likely weigh on reported revenues next year.

This dynamic, coupled with an elevated 28.19x multiple relative to expected 2027 EPS of $3.53, arguably supports a near-term Hold rating on Coca-Cola. This is also evident from the $99.40 12-month average price target set by Wall Street analysts, implying downside.

Despite the limited capital gain potential, I believe Coca-Cola shares remain interesting for growth investors looking to diversify away from the AI growth theme. After the recent share price rally, however, this diversification now comes at a steep price, in my opinion.

data.title: Lockheed Martin Stock (LMT) Looks Attractive Despite the Budget Debate
data.description:
Lockheed Martin (LMT) stock looks attractive to me despite uncertainty over next year’s defense budget, because its existing contracts provide strong revenue visibility. The aerospace and defense contractor holds a record $292 billion backlog. CEO Jim Taiclet said the F-35 framework “strengthens the way we can plan and invest in the F-35 enterprise.”

Investors are questioning next year’s Pentagon spending, but production ramps are already underway. I remain bullish on LMT stock because those commitments can support earnings for years, all while shares trade near 17.67x next year’s estimates.

Q3 Shows the Production Ramps Working

Lockheed’s Q3 shows its production ramps working at full speed. Results showed sales rising 11% to $20.7 billion. Earnings per share (EPS) increased 15% to $7.97, and free cash flow (FCF) reached $3 billion. Backlog jumped 27% sequentially to $292 billion. All four segments grew.

Management raised its sales, EPS, and FCF outlook for the second consecutive quarter. I think that broad performance deserves more attention than speculation about one budget.

Missiles and Fire Control led the advance. Sales and operating profit both rose 24% as production of Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) increased. Ramps in Guided Multiple Launch Rocket Systems (GMLRS) and Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) also contributed. The missile-segment backlog reached $142.5 billion, up from $46.7 billion at year-end.

The PAC-3 MSE multiyear award totals roughly $58.6 billion, supporting capacity expansion from roughly 600 interceptors annually toward 2,000 by 2030. The seven-year THAAD award is worth up to $35 billion and targets capacity growth from 96 to 400 annually. These ramps still have considerable distance to run.

The opportunity is broadening too. The U.S. Army’s September PrSM Increment 2 award carries a ceiling of $1.2 billion. Extended range (ER) GMLRS received approval to move into production and fielding after successful operational tests.

A recent Navy contract advances PAC-3’s integration with Aegis, opening another potential market. That integration remains under development. However, it illustrates how existing technology can reach additional customers without starting a weapons program from scratch.

The Budget Debate Does Not Erase Demand

The budget debate does not erase demand for Lockheed’s products, in my view. LMT fell 6.9% after Democrats won Congress as investors questioned Trump’s proposed $1.5 trillion 2027 defense budget. Spending could fall materially below that request. Jefferies expects something closer to the House’s $1.15 trillion proposal. Greater scrutiny could delay orders or alter priorities.

Still, a smaller budget increase leaves substantial scope for procurement. Restocking depleted missile inventories remains necessary after years of elevated usage.

The backlog provides a useful perspective. Lockheed expects about 60% to become revenue beyond the next 24 months. That is an unusually long period of visibility. Backlog does not guarantee cash, and future appropriations still matter. Nevertheless, the company is expanding factories against multiyear commitments.

Longer contracts also help suppliers order materials and commit workers earlier. That planning can reduce disruption and improve factory efficiency as output rises. PAC-3 and THAAD capacity is still growing, while PrSM and ER GMLRS are moving into larger-scale production. More output can lift profits even without higher margins.

Allied demand adds another source of orders. These programs span administrations and rely on established manufacturing capabilities that cannot be replaced quickly.

It’s also worth noting that October’s F-35 framework covers 850 U.S. aircraft over 10 years, plus international orders and sustainment. Total production would remain around 156 jets annually. Congressional authorization and appropriations are required before final contracts can be awarded. If completed, the agreement should improve supplier planning and manufacturing efficiency.

There is also an immediate funding issue. Lockheed warned that Lot 20 costs exceeded current authorization and funding. Further delays could pressure cash flow. I take that seriously, but it concerns funding execution for an established platform with decades of expected service ahead.

LMT’s Valuation Looks Reasonable for the Visibility

Lockheed’s valuation looks reasonable considering the visibility discussed above. At today’s price, consensus EPS of $30.69 implies 19.17x 2026 earnings. Forecasts of $33.28 for 2027 and $36.06 for 2028 imply 17.67x and 16.31x. Consensus assumes roughly 8% annual EPS growth in both years. Delivering those estimates would steadily reduce the multiple at today’s price.

That is close to the S&P 500’s (SPX) 17.7x forward multiple. What attracts me is the quality of Lockheed’s prospective earnings. Missile-defense systems and fighter aircraft serve requirements that survive elections. Space systems and nuclear deterrence also require support across successive administrations. High qualification costs and specialized supply chains protect established suppliers.

If production ramps up faster than current assumptions, earnings estimates could rise without investors needing a more generous valuation.

Fixed-price charges could absorb some gains, while supplier bottlenecks could delay deliveries. Easing geopolitical tensions might also reduce future orders. I think the existing production commitments provide a substantial cushion, although execution remains essential. In any case, I believe Lockheed Martin’s investment case should remain robust and rather predictable throughout the medium term.

If the market begins to recognize that the risks currently facing the company may not be as significant as they seem, I believe the stock could see further upside.

Conclusion

I remain bullish because Lockheed’s investment case extends beyond next year’s budget negotiations. The company is already producing more weapons against years of orders. Political changes can affect funding schedules, but the strategic requirements remain. At 17.67x 2027 earnings, I think investors receive attractive visibility, with upside if expanding production lifts earnings above consensus.

Before we discuss each, a quick note: Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) can have payout ratios that look very high relative to earnings, but depreciation and other non-cash costs drag earnings down. So VICI paid out roughly 74% of its AFFO per share in the third quarter ($0.46 dividend vs. $0.62 AFFO). Its Q3 2026 earnings per share (EPS) was $0.31.

data.title: PayPal’s (PYPL) Turnaround Still Needs Proof
data.description:
PayPal’s (PYPL) turnaround still needs more proof, even after its Q3 FY2026 report showed higher adjusted earnings per share (EPS) and an improved full-year outlook. PayPal Holdings operates a global digital-payments network spanning its PayPal and Venmo wallets, branded checkout, Braintree payment processing, credit products, and other merchant services. At the end of 2025, its network connected 440 million active accounts across roughly 200 markets.

There is progress. PayPal’s Q3 FY2026 revenue increased 2% year-over-year to $8.58 billion; transaction margin dollars rose 2% to $4 billion.  Non-GAAP EPS climbed 8% to $1.45, and total payment volume (TPV) also advanced 6% to $487.1 billion.

Still, revenue fell short of Wall Street’s roughly $8.71 billion estimate, while the company’s most important branded checkout business remained sluggish. That tension keeps me neutral on PYPL with a Hold rating. 

PayPal’s EPS Growth Doesn’t Tell the Whole Story

PayPal’s EPS growth doesn’t tell the whole story, especially when you look at its underlying profitability. Non-GAAP EPS rose 8% to $1.45, above the $1.31 consensus estimate, and management raised its full-year adjusted EPS forecast to about $5.60 from roughly $5.38 previously, which is encouraging.

Yet looking above EPS makes the picture less convincing. Non-GAAP net income declined 3% year-over-year to $1.25 billion, while GAAP net income fell 14% to $1.07 billion. PayPal’s share count has also fallen sharply: shares outstanding were down 8.8% year-over-year as of early November. In other words, repurchases are helping per-share earnings grow faster than the underlying profit pool.

This does not make the EPS growth meaningless. Buybacks create value when shares are repurchased cheaply. Yet a lasting rerating probably requires revenue and transaction margins to accelerate as well. Freedom Capital Markets analyst Mikhail Paramonov made a similar point when he downgraded PYPL to Hold in early November, arguing that recent EPS growth reflected expense discipline and a lower share count rather than a clear acceleration in the core business.

Branded Checkout Remains the Missing Piece

Branded checkout remains the missing piece in PayPal’s turnaround, and it’s the main reason I’m reluctant to become bullish. Online branded checkout payment volume growth has remained around 1%–2% for four consecutive quarters, and management expects a similar pace through the fourth quarter.

Branded checkout has historically been one of PayPal’s more valuable businesses. The company itself acknowledges intense competition across digital wallets and payment methods, with consumers and merchants able to choose among bank products, card networks and competing payment technologies.

There are brighter spots. Braintree Total Payment Volume (TPV) grew about 10% in Q3 FY2026, while Venmo produced mid-teens volume growth. Management also expects financial services to contribute more than 20% of transaction margin dollars in 2026, with double-digit growth.

These businesses do not eliminate the need to stabilize PayPal-branded checkout. Until product updates begin taking share or meaningfully accelerating growth, I think investors should keep questioning whether the broader transformation is changing PayPal’s competitive position or merely improving efficiency around a slow-growing core.

PayPal’s Cash Flow and Buybacks Provide Support

PayPal’s cash flow and buybacks provide some reassurance, making a bearish rating difficult to justify. The company generated $1.43 billion in free cash flow (FCF) and $2.05 billion in adjusted FCF in Q3 FY2026. Management now expects at least $6.5 billion in adjusted FCF for the Fiscal year 2026.

PayPal also repurchased roughly $1.5 billion of stock during the quarter and $6 billion over the trailing 12 months and continued returning capital to shareholders, with its board declaring a quarterly dividend of $0.14 per share.

The caveat here is that Q3 FY 2026 FCF fell 17% year-over-year from $1.72 billion. Even so, PayPal’s ability to generate several billion dollars of annual cash flow gives management considerable room to reduce the share count and invest in the turnaround. This is what keeps PayPal out of Sell territory for me.

PayPal’s Valuation

At its current price, PayPal trades at roughly 10.6x forward price-to-earnings (P/E) and 11x trailing earnings. This is a substantial compression from earlier years. PayPal traded at roughly 18.2x forward P/E at the end of FY 2024, and its five-year average forward P/E is 16x. The current multiple is also far below Visa’s (V) forward P/E of about 28.1x and Mastercard’s (MA) 32.7x.

The discount makes PYPL look inexpensive, but I would not call it obviously mispriced. Visa and Mastercard have different business models and stronger recent growth profiles, while PayPal still needs to demonstrate that branded checkout can reaccelerate. The low multiple already reflects this, which supports a Hold rather than either extreme.

What Could Change My Hold Thesis?

A sustained rebound in branded checkout could change my Hold thesis and push me toward a Buy rating, particularly if PayPal pairs it with stronger transaction-margin growth. Faster monetization of Venmo and financial services would strengthen that case. Management’s plan to deliver at least $1.5 billion of gross run-rate cost savings over the next two to three years could provide another lever if those savings translate into durable earnings rather than being fully reinvested.

The downside case is equally clear. Continued market-share pressure in checkout, weaker consumer spending, or further deterioration in FCF would make the low valuation look less like an opportunity and more like a value trap. 

Wall Street’s Outlook for PYPL

Wall Street remains cautious on PYPL, with a Hold consensus rating based on three Buys, 22 Holds, and four Sells over the past three months. At $57.60, the average analyst price target implies about 2.77% downside from the last price of $59.24.

Recent analyst revisions reflect similar hesitation about PayPal’s turnaround. Freedom Capital analyst Mikhail Paramonov downgraded the stock from Buy to Hold and cut his price target from $72 to $63 as the company’s core business continues to struggle to stabilize. TD Cowen analyst Bryan Bergin raised his target from $59 to $60 but kept a Hold rating, noting progress in Venmo and PayPal’s financial services business.

Conclusion

Both analysts see room for improvement, but neither sees enough evidence to justify a Buy rating, and I share their caution. PayPal’s attractive valuation and cash generation offer some reassurance, but until branded checkout improves meaningfully, I believe a Hold remains the more reasonable stance.

data.title: These 2 Dividend Stocks Yield Up to 12% — Bank of America Sees a Buying Opportunity
data.description:
Last week was a wild ride for Wall Street, as investors struggled to make sense of a political shake-up that could have serious consequences for the stock market.

The Democrats’ decisive win in the midterm elections, which handed them control of both the House and Senate, raised concerns about tighter regulations, particularly for tech companies investing heavily in AI and data centers. With fears of higher operating costs and restrictions on future construction adding to existing worries about stretched valuations, investors wasted little time cutting their exposure to riskier assets. By Friday’s closing bell, the S&P 500 had lost 2.7% for the week, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq suffered a 3.4% drop.

When market turbulence starts making investors nervous, many begin looking for ways to make their portfolios more defensive. One popular approach is turning to dividend-paying stocks, which can provide a steady stream of income even when share prices are heading in the wrong direction.

Of course, dividends offer no guarantee against losses, and companies can reduce their payouts if financial conditions deteriorate. This is why investors should look for stocks that combine attractive dividend yields with solid financial fundamentals.

Enter Bank of America analyst Derek Hewett, who has pinpointed two dividend stocks he believes are worth buying at current prices. Both have struggled since the beginning of the year, but they now offer dividend yields of up to 12%. Despite their disappointing stock performance, Hewett sees reasons to remain confident in their financial strength and longer-term prospects, along with the potential for a rebound in their share prices.

In fact, Hewett has plenty of company on Wall Street; both dividend stocks carry Strong Buy consensus ratings, according to the TipRanks database. Let’s see what makes these two names worth considering.

Barings BDC (BBDC)

Bank of America’s first pick, Barings BDC, operates in a corner of the financial market that many everyday investors rarely encounter. Rather than lending money to consumers or large corporations, the company provides financing to middle-market businesses, primarily through privately negotiated loans. These investments generate interest income, much of which eventually makes its way into shareholders’ pockets through quarterly dividend payments.

What makes Barings BDC particularly appealing is the combination of its income-generating portfolio and the financial backing of Barings, a global investment manager specializing in private credit. The company also benefits from credit support arrangements with its external manager, Barings, which provide protection against certain investment losses under specified conditions, although their coverage is limited.

And judging by its latest earnings report, released last Thursday, the company’s financial position remains relatively steady. Third-quarter investment income totaled $64.3 million, while net investment income reached $27.2 million, or $0.26 per share, matching Wall Street’s expectations. Meanwhile, net assets resulting from operations increased by $24.6 million, equivalent to $0.24 per share.

Then there’s the dividend, arguably the biggest reason income investors might want to take a closer look. With a quarterly distribution of $0.26 per share, Barings BDC offers an annualized payout of $1.04, translating into a forward dividend yield of about 12%.

So why has the stock lost about 6% since the beginning of the year? Part of the answer lies in concerns about credit quality and the possibility that lower interest rates could squeeze future investment income. An increase in nonaccrual loans, where borrowers are no longer generating recognized interest income, has added to those worries.

Yet, while these concerns have weighed on investor sentiment, Bank of America’s Derek Hewett sees a more encouraging picture emerging from the company’s latest quarterly results, suggesting the market may be overlooking some of its underlying strengths.

“Barings BDC reported a relatively good quarter as core EPS was in line with Consensus, NAV/share was stable, and the portfolio was modestly higher. While nonaccruals increased, overall levels remain well below peer levels, and the CSA adds another layer of protection for shareholders. Despite the more complex operating backdrop, we think BBDC is well positioned to generate attractive risk-adjusted returns,” Hewett opined.

Based on that confidence, Hewett assigns BBDC shares a Buy rating and a $10 price target, pointing to about 16% upside from current levels. (To watch Hewett’s track record, click here)

And the broader analyst community appears to share much of that confidence. Three of the four analysts covering BBDC recommend buying the stock, while the remaining expert prefers to sit on the fence. Together, those recommendations give the high-yield dividend stock a Strong Buy consensus rating, with an average 12-month price target of $9.63, suggesting another 11.40% in potential share price gains.

Add the stock’s 12% forward dividend yield to the equation, and investors could be looking at a combined potential return of 23.4% over the next year. (See BBDC stock forecast)

Sixth Street Specialty Lending (TSLX)

Next on Bank of America’s list is Sixth Street Specialty Lending, another business development company that has built its reputation around lending to middle-market businesses. But there’s an important difference in how this lender approaches the market. Rather than competing for every available deal, Sixth Street focuses on finding opportunities where it can negotiate favorable terms while keeping a close eye on the possibility that borrowers might run into financial trouble.

The company primarily invests in senior secured loans, which generally give lenders priority over other creditors if a borrower defaults. It also draws on the resources of its parent organization, Sixth Street, a global investment firm overseeing more than $140 billion in assets and committed capital. That combination of lending expertise and access to privately negotiated transactions helps explain why Bank of America considers TSLX particularly well-positioned among its peers.

And its latest quarterly results, released last Tuesday, provided some evidence that the strategy is holding up. Sixth Street reported third-quarter adjusted net investment income of $0.44 per share, matching Wall Street’s expectations. Total investment income reached $98.96 million, exceeding analysts’ forecasts by $1.06 million.

For dividend investors, the appeal is easy to understand. Sixth Street recently declared another quarterly base dividend of $0.42 per share, equivalent to $1.68 annually. At the recent share price of $17.65, that works out to a forward dividend yield of about 9.5%. The company also announced a supplemental distribution of $0.01 per share, providing a little extra income beyond its regular payout.

Still, TSLX shares have lost nearly 19% since the beginning of the year, with much of the damage occurring in February. The selloff reflected growing concerns about private credit, particularly lenders’ exposure to software companies facing potential disruption from AI. Investors worried that weakening borrowers could translate into loan losses, while broader uncertainty surrounding credit quality made BDC stocks less appealing. Lower interest rates and tighter lending spreads have also raised concerns about future investment income.

Bank of America’s Hewett, however, believes Sixth Street’s latest results demonstrate why the company deserves a more favorable assessment than its recent stock performance might suggest.

“Sixth Street reported a solid quarter, with core EPS in line with BofA/Consensus. Positively, net loan growth turned positive, the portfolio yield rose, and non-accruals declined modestly. NAV/share was largely stable. That said, new-deal spreads compressed and the watch list increased. We continue to view TSLX as one of the best positioned BDCs given its late-cycle focus and proprietary origination platform,” Hewett noted.

Hewett backs that confidence with a Buy rating and a $19.50 price target, implying a 10.5% upside from the current share price.

Overall, Wall Street appears largely convinced that Sixth Street has more to offer investors. Five of the six analysts following TSLX recommend buying its shares, with only one maintaining a Hold rating. This translates into a Strong Buy consensus, while the average price target of $18.92 suggests a 7.2% gain over the next 12 months. The picture becomes more appealing when dividends enter the equation, bringing the potential annual return to nearly 16.7%. (See TSLX stock forecast)
